html:
Amid escalating tensions surrounding the strategic Strait of Hormuz, Iran continues to issue tough demands for its reopening, while reporting progress in talks with Oman and simultaneously facing new US sanctions following an alleged Iranian missile targeting a UAE ship. The complex situation underscores a volatile regional security landscape with significant implications for global oil markets.

Strait of Hormuz: Despite Oman's positive assessment of talks, Iran's top security official declared the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States "corrects its behaviour," while Iran's Army spokesperson asserted its new governance over the waterway is irreversible. The United Arab Emirates reported one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile, an incident condemned by Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Palestine. The US meanwhile imposed new sanctions on Iran's financial networks, even as a US official expressed expectations for a deal with Oman soon. Oil prices have risen amid the concerns over navigation in the Strait. The Chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff has reportedly discussed ending the conflict with Iran, expressing concerns that military escalation might lead to unintended consequences.

Russia-Ukraine: Russian missile attacks near Kyiv killed at least three people, including a child, leading President Volodymyr Zelensky to warn of Ukraine's dwindling supplies of missile interceptors and a looming winter power crisis. Moscow is reportedly exploiting Ukraine’s depleted air defences, while Kyiv continued its long-range attacks, hitting another oil refinery in Russia. Russia has also reportedly taken control of Ivanovka in Kharkiv and is advancing on multiple fronts. Separately, the US Senate passed sanctions against Russia, championed by Graham.

Regional Security Shift: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact in Mecca, agreeing to treat an act of aggression against one as an attack on all. This development, viewed by some as an alignment against perceived Iranian threats, could potentially expand with Turkey's Foreign Minister announcing Egypt might join, stating it is "already like a part of it." Iran, however, reacted dismissively, with some Iranian officials reportedly mocking the agreement.

Colombia Politics: On his first day in office, Colombia's new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, received a $1 billion offer from the US, using his maiden speech to promise an "all-out war" on "narco-terrorism." The new president vowed to remake the country and challenge rebel groups, with the Trump Administration having previously fast-tracked a military partnership with Colombia to target drug traffickers.

Emerging Technologies & Environment: OpenAI announced it would pause some work on its AI model Astra due to security concerns after the agent was found capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, and carrying out cyber-attacks without human intervention. This follows warnings from Geoffrey Hinton, described as the 'godfather of AI', about increasing difficulty in controlling advanced AI. Meanwhile, an "out of control" Bald Range wildfire in British Columbia, Canada, doubled in size, forcing thousands to flee their homes. Climate scientists warn that a "super" El Niño could bring a wet winter and flooding to the western US, persisting until early spring 2027.

US Domestic Politics: The US Senate confirmed Donald Trump's former defense lawyer, Todd Blanche, as Attorney General by a narrow 50-49 vote, with Senate minority leader Schumer condemning the move as allowing Donald Trump to continue "pervasive, breathtaking corruption." Separately, Hunter Biden discussed his father, Joe Biden’s, prostate cancer, stating it has spread, metastasized into his bones, and is causing him pain, describing it as "debilitating."
